title: Reimagining the Human Side of AI: A Conversation with Suzanne Kirkendall
summary: Explore how behavioral science can help organizations build trusted AI, preserve human judgment, and create meaningful value as AI reshapes the workplace.
body_markdown:
*By Suzanne Kirkendall, Allie Blaising, and Teng Liu*


We often think AI adoption is the goal. But recent research highlights what can happen when AI adoption outpaces AI strategy - from[workslop and botsitting](https://www.glean.com/work-ai-institute/reports/work-ai-index) degrading work satisfaction to[unchecked AI trust and errors](https://fortune.com/2026/08/04/your-best-work-ai-bare-minimum-no-free-time/) hurting business metrics. In other words, more AI doesn't automatically mean more value and behavioral science can help explain that gap. Whether and how people actually use AI depends on trust, identity, social norms, and incentives, not just on what the technology can do. And it’s a two-way street: we shape how AI gets adopted, even as AI quietly shapes how we think, work, and relate to each other.


Upwork recently connected with Suzanne as part of Reimagining Work, our lecture series bringing together expert perspectives on the present and future of work.[Suzanne Kirkendall](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kirkendallsuzanne) is the Founder and[CEO of Verelon](https://www.verelongroup.com/) , a behavioral science consultancy helping organizations apply the science of human behavior as AI reshapes work. During the conversation, she explored what behavioral science can teach us about building AI people trust, driving meaningful value, and preserving the human relationships and judgment critical to how we work.


**Allie: From a behavioral science perspective, where have we gone wrong in assuming that making AI available will naturally translate into value?**


The biggest mistake is that we keep building for a “rational” user who doesn't exist. The assumption underneath “availability equals value” is that people just need to know: if the tool works and we explain it well, adoption will automatically follow. But knowing and doing are different things. We all know how much sleep we should get and we don't get it.


When people don't adopt something, a knowledge gap is rarely the reason. The real drivers tend to be things like identity (this threatens how I see my role), control (this makes me feel less in charge of my work), or plain effort (it's buried three clicks deep and I can't be bothered). Those reasons might not look perfectly logical on paper, but they drive behavior, so they're the reality we have to design for.


The practical shift: diagnose accurately before you jump into fixing. When a feature isn't being received as expected, the reflex is to explain it more, louder, or differently. Instead, go look at what's blocking the behavior first. Sometimes the fix is a simple menu structure tweak, not a whole new messaging campaign.


**Teng: As AI makes it easier to offload more of our thinking and work, how should we decide what we should continue doing ourselves?**


This is not a new worry! Ancient philosophers feared that writing would ruin human memory. But we’ve offloaded navigation to GPS and phone numbers to our contacts list, and we adjusted. Our job now is to decide what and how we adapt, rather than passively letting it happen to us.


My advice for the workplace is to make it an explicit team decision: what work we’re fine turning into an AI-driven production line, and what work we’re protecting because it builds judgment. Take qualitative research. AI can summarize a stack of interview transcripts in seconds, and that's useful. But the skill and insight you develop by sitting with those transcripts yourself can't be replaced by reading the summary. If you never do that type of work manually, you lose the ability to judge whether AI's output is any good.


This matters most for people early in their careers, who are still building those muscles. But it applies at every level. Decide together, say it out loud, and revisit it as the tools change.


**Allie: How is trust in AI different from trust in another person? What should product builders take away from that distinction?**


We give humans context. If a colleague drops the ball, we think they're stressed, but they're usually great, and we adjust how much we lean on them for now without writing them off as a person. Trust in another human has shades of gray and is repairable.


We judge machines in black and white. It either works, or it broke once and now it's broken. Rebuilding trust after a machine fails is much harder, because we don't extend machines the context we extend people.


AI makes this stranger, because we treat it as a tool and a sort of mind at the same time. We have feelings about it, we get offended by it, we care how it interacts with our relationships. Nobody has feelings like that about their calculator. So AI gets the emotional weight of a person and the failure tolerance of software, which is a hard combination to build trust for.


For people building products, a few suggestions follow from this understanding. Show the work, not just the answer; even when the output is identical, revealing what’s inside the black box increases comfort. Make actions reversible and easy to override. Signal confidence honestly: if a feature is imperfect, say how, so people know what to lean on it for and don't get burned by inflated expectations. Watch what people do rather than relying on what they say, because we have poor access to our own reasons for how we behave. And introduce new capabilities where the stakes are low, so people can build up trust through exposure before relying on it for anything important.


**Teng: As AI makes it possible to produce more work faster, how might that change our expectations of what good performance looks like, and what should organizations be cautious about?**


Speed is easy to measure, and quality often isn't, so speed defaults into being the performance standard. Even if a team agrees that providing thoughtful feedback deserves real human effort, they often fall into praising whoever turns things around fastest. People do what gets acknowledged, not what the team said in a meeting, so rewarding speed means favoring AI output over human thinking.


There’s another risk that shows up later. Organizational psychology tells us people are motivated by progress, mastery, and ownership of work they can point to. When the job shifts from doing the work to supervising a machine's output, those experiences can thin out. Volume climbs even as the person's connection to the work drops, which is the pattern behind reports of AI-heavy workflows reducing satisfaction while output rises.


So be very intentional about what you celebrate. And protect the parts of the job where people build skill and feel their own progress. Increasing output while eroding motivation is a recipe for a disengaged workforce.


**Allie: Most conversations about AI focus on the relationship between humans and machines. How is AI changing the way humans relate to each other? What should this mean for leaders?**


Two interesting things are happening at once. 1.) AI is resetting our expectations of each other, and 2.) it's creating new social signals we haven't agreed on yet.


On expectations: AI is available at midnight, never gets annoyed when you ask the same question four times, and rarely pushes back hard. Real people have friction: they take a day to respond, they show up grumpy sometimes. That friction has always been normal, but now next to a chatbot it starts to feel like a flaw.


On signals: ask anyone how it feels to receive an obviously unedited AI message and you'll hear disrespected, transactional, not worth their time. The strange part is the content can be correct, or even better-written than the person would have managed manually, but it still damages the relationship more than a slower, shorter, clearly human reply would have.


For leaders, there are three things you can do to help with this. First, name the norm as a team: decide out loud when AI-assisted communication is fine (a one-to-many update) and when it isn't (feedback, thank-yous, anything relational), because right now we're all judging each other by our own invisible rules, and no two people have the same one. Second, for relational work, start and finish in your own words; AI can help in the middle, refining thoughts you've already put down in your own words. Third, make sure what you reward matches the norm you set. If you say you value thoughtful communication but celebrate the fastest replies, people will do what aligns with the reward, not the words.


A year from now the tools will be unrecognizable. Our working relationships will still run on the same human fundamentals they always have: attention, effort, and respect.

[Suzanne Kirkendall](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kirkendallsuzanne/) **** is the Founder and CEO of[Verelon](http://www.verelongroup.com/) , a behavioral science consultancy helping organizations apply the science of human behavior as AI reshapes work. She previously led North America for BVA Nudge Consulting and co-founded the Social Science division at McCann Health. She holds an MPH from Columbia University, is a SHRM Senior Certified Professional, and publishes peer-reviewed research on behavior change. She guest lectures at graduate schools including Columbia Business School and Penn.

[Allie Blaising](https://www.linkedin.com/in/allie-blaising-ms/) is a Senior Lead User Experience Researcher at Upwork, where she leads customer research that shapes business decisions across Upwork, with a recent focus on Small Business Growth and AI product initiatives. She holds a Master’s in Science from University of Pennsylvania.


[Teng Liu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tengliu/) **** is an economist at Upwork, where he studies how AI and technological change are transforming the labor market and reshaping skill demand. He holds a Ph.D. in economics from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and specializes in labor market dynamics and quantitative research. His work informs Upwork’s insights on workforce shifts, economic opportunity, and policy.
